newsitem.title: UK: Risk of cen bank gold sales seen dwindling.
newsitem.headline: Risk of cen bank gold sales seen dwindling.

text.p: The likelihood of central banks selling gold to meet economic rules for European Monetary Union (EMU) will diminish with time, a Bank of England official said on Tuesday.

Terry Smeeton, head of the UK central bank's foreign exchange division, made the comments in remarks prepared for delivery at the Fifth Central Banking Conference in London. "...The window of opportunity for gold sales in terms of using the book profits to reduce external debt in the way Belgium has done is going to close in about a year's time and so the threat to the gold market...should be time expired," he said.
Smeeton said that if the EMU was still "readying for launch" in a year's time, central banks might be wary of selling a dependable asset when a potentially hazardous future beckoned.
"Central banks must always keep a wary eye on an uncertain future...the risk of central bank sales should not be exaggerated," he said.
Also likely to influence gold prices next year was a higher level of gold interest rates which developed more than a year ago and was likely to continue, he said.
This could encourage a revival in investment interest in gold as fund managers run gold portfolios alongside some of their current investments.
"In the generally low interest rate environment...around the world it means that gold interest rates are not uncompetitive from an investment point of view," Smeeton said.
In the past year gold interest rates have often been well over one percent for one year, notably higher than previously.

But he noted that the gold market had not had "an auspicious year" after a rally early in 1996 petered out, the national Bank of Belgium sold from reserves and rumours of other central bank sales and threats of sales by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) hung over the market.
A Bank of England survey among gold's market makers showed very similar turnover to two years previously except that there was a shift away from spot business towards forwards.
He added that London's relatively stagnant position was not worse than elsewhere.
Comex gold futures and options volume was five percent lower than during a comparable survey period two years earlier.
